definitions.definition: The regular walking pilgrimage to Paṇḍharpūr, above all for the Āṣāḍhī and Kārtikī ekādaśīs, made in singing companies (diṇḍī) behind the saints' palanquins; keeping it for life is what makes one a Vārkarī.
One who keeps the vārī to Paṇḍharpūr; a member of the Vārkarī sampradāya, marked by the tuḷsī necklace, vegetarianism, the Ekādaśī fast and the name.
A company of Vārkarī pilgrims walking and singing together behind a flag, with cymbals (ṭāḷ) and drum, as a unit of the vārī.
The palanquin carrying the silver sandals (pādukā) of a saint — above all Jñāneśvar's from Āḷandī and Tukārām's from Dehu — at the head of the vārī.
A rite on the way to Paṇḍharpūr in which a horse (held to carry the saint unseen) runs in a circle round the assembled pilgrims.
The 'unbroken' metre of Marathi devotional song and the song composed in it — the form of the Vārkarī saints' poetry, sung in bhajan and kīrtan.
The Marathi verse-form of the Jñāneśvarī, Amṛtānubhava and Eknāthī Bhāgavat, also used in women's grinding songs.
The verse form of the classic Mahānubhāva poems.
Congregational singing of abhaṅgas and the name with cymbals and drum, the daily and nightly practice of Vārkarī groups.
Devotional song to Rāma sung in company.
Worship in general; also the second, inner instruction given after śaraṇ (usage to verify).
The necklace of tuḷsī (basil) beads put on at initiation into the Vārkarī way; its wearer (māḷkarī) vows vegetarianism, abstinence, the Ekādaśī fast and the name.
The Lord of Paṇḍharpūr (also Viṭhobā, Pāṇḍuraṅga, Viṭhāī 'mother Viṭṭhala'), a form of Kṛṣṇa who stands on the brick Puṇḍalīka threw him, hands on hips; for some saints one with Śiva as well.

literal: (popularly) 'standing on a brick' (viṭ + ṭhala); other derivations exist

definitions.definition: 'Mother': the Vārkarīs' name for Viṭṭhala and for Jñāneśvar, expressing God and the saint as mother to the devotee.
A married woman's mother's home; the saints call Paṇḍharpūr their māher, with Viṭṭhala and Rakhumāī as parents and the saints as kin.
'The gift of grace': the closing prayer of the Jñāneśvarī for the good of all beings, sung at the end of Vārkarī gatherings.
'The king of paths': Jñāneśvar's name in Jñāneśvarī 6 for the Nāth yoga of kuṇḍalinī's awakening and ascent (summary only).
Living samādhi: the saint, still alive, sits in meditation in a chamber that is then sealed, and is held to remain present there — above all Jñāneśvar at Āḷandī.

equivalents.note: the Tamil Siddhar 'cīva camāti' is described in the same terms; different lineage and context

definitions.definition: 'The play of consciousness': the name later given to Jñāneśvar's teaching in the Amṛtānubhava that the one reality sports as the world without change or second.
Dramatic allegorical folk song in which a village character (scorpion-bitten man, Jogī, madwoman) carries a hidden spiritual meaning; perfected by Eknāth.
The Vārkarī mantra, given to Tukārām in his dream-initiation and chanted by all Vārkarīs.
A week of continuous singing of the name and reading of the Jñāneśvarī or Gāthā in a village, ending in kīrtan and a common meal.
The saint, in whom God is present; the saints' company is the true tīrtha and their feet are sought above liberation.
The good person whose company (satsaṅg) gives discernment; greater than the Lord himself in Rāma's teaching to Śabarī.
Worldly household life; the saints teach that prapañca and paramārtha (the highest aim) can be joined.
Worldly life, to be conducted with vigilance and effort together with the pursuit of the highest.
The world, one of the four eternal realities: made of māyā, distinct from souls, deities and Parameśvara.
The highest aim — God and liberation — pursued within household life.
The spiritual goal, which the Dāsbodh teaches alongside skilful worldly life.
The five incarnations of Parameśvara: Śrī Kṛṣṇa, Dattātreya, Cāṅgadeva Rāüḷ, Govindaprabhu and Cakradhar.
The one Supreme, distinct from souls, deities and world, who alone grants liberation and incarnates as the five Kṛṣṇas.
The gods of the Vedas and Purāṇas, one of the four realities: powerful beings who can give worldly fruit but are themselves bound and cannot liberate; not to be worshipped.
The soul, one of the four eternal realities: countless, bound by ignorance, liberated only by Parameśvara's grace.
A place sanctified by the presence or touch of one of the incarnations, visited and venerated by Mahānubhāvas.
The renunciant's continual wandering, not staying long in one place.
Living by begged food, part of the renunciant discipline Cakradhar enjoined.
A parable by which Cakradhar illustrated a teaching, collected in the Dṛṣṭāntapāṭh.
One of the secret scripts in which the Mahānubhāvas long preserved their scriptures from outsiders.
Taking refuge in Kṛṣṇa alone, to the exclusion of every other deity and of Vedic rites; the defining principle of Śaṅkaradeva's dharma.
The four things of the dharma: the name (nāma), God (deva), the guru and the community of devotees (bhakta).
An Ekaśaraṇa monastery-institution under a sattrādhikār, with a prayer hall, the sanctum holding the book, resident celibate or married devotees, and lay disciples attached to it.
The village prayer hall where the community gathers for the name (nām-prasaṅga), reading, drama and council.
The sanctum of a sattra or nāmghar in which the guru-āsana with the sacred book is kept.
The tiered wooden throne, often borne by carved figures, on which the sacred book (Bhāgavata or Kīrtana-ghoṣā) is enthroned and worshipped in place of an image.
The head of a sattra, who gives initiation (śaraṇ) and guides its disciples.
A celibate devotee who lives in the sattra, devoted wholly to worship; the ideal set by Mādhavadeva.
A devotee; also the resident monks of a sattra; as bhakta, one of the four real things.
Congregational worship in the nāmghar by singing the name and verses of the Kīrtana-ghoṣā and Nām-ghoṣā, led by a nām-lagowā.
The staging of an aṅkīyā nāṭ in the nāmghar as an act of worship.
The devotional rāga songs of Śaṅkaradeva and Mādhavadeva in Brajabuli.
Śaṅkaradeva's genre of one-act devotional plays in Brajabuli, performed as bhāonā.
Any of the four groupings of sattras formed after Mādhavadeva (Brahma, Puruṣa, Kāla, Nikā).
Title of Śaṅkaradeva (and Mādhavadeva) in the tradition, which is therefore also called Mahāpuruṣīyā.
The literary song-language (a blend of Maithili with Assamese or Bengali) used for bargīts and aṅkīyā nāṭs, and in Bengal for Vaiṣṇava lyrics.
The director-narrator of an aṅkīyā nāṭ who sings, dances, introduces and explains the action and stays on stage throughout.
Śaraṇ: the initiation by which one takes refuge in Kṛṣṇa, the name, the guru and the devotees, given by a sattrādhikār.
The name 'Rāma', greater than both the formless and the embodied Brahman, mediating between them, the one support in the Kali age and the ferrying mantra Śiva gives the dying at Kāśī.

equivalents.note: the Rāma name is one of the forms the tāraka mantra takes (Kāśī), not the whole of the tāraka doctrine

definitions.definition: The six-syllable Rāma mantra (rāṃ rāmāya namaḥ) given at Rāmānandī initiation.

notes: Form of the initiation mantra as commonly reported; verify against Rāmānandī manuals.

definitions.definition: Rāma as the supreme person who keeps every bound of dharma — as son, brother, husband and king.
Rāma's reign as the pattern of a righteous order, free of bodily, divine and elemental suffering, where all keep their dharma and love one another.
The diseases of the mind: delusion the root, lust as wind, greed as phlegm, anger as bile, with jealousy, pride and the rest; cured by Rāma's grace through the guru, faith, restraint and devotion.
A devotee who contemplates the sweet, intimate love-play of Sītā and Rāma as a companion (sakhī).
A connoisseur of the pair's love (rasa) in Vṛndāvana; used of the Rādhāvallabha and Haridāsī poets.
As in the Rādhāvallabha usage: one who tastes the rasa of the nikuñja.
A renunciant Rāmānandī ascetic, as distinct from the householder and the rasik.
Love, the supreme principle: the divine pair are two forms of hita, and hita is also the path and the goal; Harivaṃśa is its embodiment.

equivalents.note: hita is prema taken as the ultimate principle itself, not only as the devotee's highest state

notes: Distinct from trm:hita (the Upaniṣadic hitā channels).

definitions.definition: The eternal love-play of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa in the groves of Vṛndāvana, without separation, birth-story or departure.
The eternal play of the natural pair in the nikuñja.
The inner grove of Vṛndāvana where the pair's eternal play goes on.
The grove (kuñja) of the eternal pair, focus of the Haridāsī worship.
'Their happiness': the sakhī's joy lies only in the pair's joy, never in her own union.
Worship of the eternal pair in the grove as a sakhī, through song and inner service.

equivalents.note: worship of the divine couple in the Nimbārka school; the Haridāsīs stress the grove and the sakhī stance

definitions.definition: Collective temple singing of the founders' padas in fixed style as worship.
The same practice in Rādhāvallabha temples.
The devotee's stance as a companion (sahacarī) of Rādhā, serving the pair and delighting in their joy, never seeking union for herself.
The stance of the singer-witness in the grove; Svāmī Haridās is held to be the sakhī Lalitā.
The Rāma-rasik devotee's identity as a companion of Sītā in the inner Ayodhyā.
'Natural, innate': the divine pair (sahaja jorī) are eternally together by nature, never joined and never parted.

notes: Haridāsī sense only; not the Sahajiyā or Nāth sense.

definitions.definition: Public shame and family honour (kul-kī-maryādā), which Mīrā casts off for Kṛṣṇa.
'Holder of the mountain': Kṛṣṇa who lifted Govardhana; Mīrā's Giridhar Gopāl or Giridhar Nāgar, her husband and the signature of her songs.

term: śrī rām jay rām jay jay rām

definitions.definition: The thirteen-syllable (trayodaśākṣarī) Rāma mantra of the Samartha sampradāya.

native: श्रीराम जय राम जय जय राम

definitions.definition: In the Dāsbodh: The bound person sunk in the world, first of the four conditions.
In the Dāsbodh: The seeker who has turned from the world and longs for freedom.
In the Dāsbodh: The practitioner who takes up hearing, reflection and devotion under the guru.
In the Dāsbodh: The accomplished one who abides in the Self, free of doubt, still acting rightly.
The active spiritual leader Rāmdās describes: learned, tireless, organising people, teaching and protecting dharma.
Effort: Rāmdās's watchword, to be joined with devotion in both worldly and spiritual life.
Narsinh Mehta's 'true Vaiṣṇava': one who knows others' pain, helps without pride, speaks ill of none and is free of greed, deceit, lust and anger.
Worship through sound and music, joined to devotion (Tyāgarāja).
The name of God ('Viṭṭhala', 'Rāma Kṛṣṇa Hari'), the easy means that needs no rule of time, place or caste; standing a moment at God's door with the name wins the four liberations.
Rāma's name, greater than both his formless and embodied forms and the one support in Kali.
The name of Kṛṣṇa, first of the four real things and the chief means of the single refuge.
Kīrtan: a sung and spoken discourse on an abhaṅga, with the chorus singing the name, led by a kīrtankār; with bhajan the heart of Vārkarī practice.
Singing the Lord's names and deeds, with hearing (śravaṇa) the foremost of the nine devotions; the Kīrtana-ghoṣā is its text.
The embodied Rāma: the formless becomes embodied, overcome by the devotee's love; not different from the formless.
The formless, qualityless Brahman, not different from the embodied Rāma; the name mediates between them.
The formless Brahman beyond the elements, known by discrimination.
The company of the good, without which there is no discernment, and which Rāma's grace grants; first of the nine devotions taught to Śabarī.
The saints' company, asked for above liberation.

Tulsī's own list to Śabarī: saints' company, love of the Lord's stories, service to the guru, singing his qualities, mantra repetition, self-control, seeing the world full of him, contentment, and guileless trust.
The Bhāgavata's nine, each expounded in the Dāsbodh's fourth daśaka, culminating in self-offering.
The nine forms, of which hearing and singing are foremost.
Servanthood: 'I am the servant, the Lord is the master in the form of all beings' (Hanumān's model).
The servant's devotion that alone is cultivated; the erotic mood and Rādhā are not.
Exclusive devotion: the unwavering understanding 'I am the servant, the Lord is the master in the form of all'.
The Rāma name as the ferrying mantra Śiva gives those who die at Kāśī.
The degenerate age in which neither ritual, devotion nor discernment stands on its own and the name is the one support — yet the best of ages for one with faith.
'I and mine, you and yours': the power that holds all beings; a painting without colour on the void, neither simply true nor false.
Ignorance, which Jñāneśvar's Amṛtānubhava argues cannot exist in the self-luminous reality at all.
The anguish of separation from Giridhar, the wound only the wounded know.
Not real in the eternal play, where the pair are never apart; felt only within union.
Dwelling in the Lord's world, the first of the four liberations, perishable with the worlds.
Union with the Lord, the only one of the four liberations that does not perish.
The true guru who gives knowledge of the Self and removes doubt, as opposed to givers of mantras for gain or displays of power.
The true guru, the helmsman of the boat of the human body.
The coiled power whose waking and ascent Jñāneśvar describes in Jñāneśvarī 6 as the Nāths' royal road (summary only).
Strict non-harming, down to the smallest creature, required of the renunciant.
